display.aside: In a dark chamber the plant releases carbon dioxide and takes in oxygen, and in bright light those net changes reverse. That is why the take-turns idea feels convincing.
display.title: Do photosynthesis and respiration take turns?
display.belief: Photosynthesis happens in sunlight and respiration happens in darkness, so the plant switches from one to the other and only respires at night.
display.evidence: In a plant cell in bright light, the mitochondria are still taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide while the chloroplasts photosynthesise. Respiration has not switched off; light does not stop it.
display.conclusion: Respiration is continuous, day and night. Photosynthesis runs whenever light is available, so in the light both processes run at the same time in the same cell.

accessibility.description: Misconception callout: the belief that a plant respires only in darkness and photosynthesises only in light is tested against a plant cell in bright light, where mitochondria keep respiring, and corrected by stating that respiration is continuous while photosynthesis runs whenever light is available.

display.aside: Textbooks often describe plants releasing oxygen for animals, so the plant's own need for that oxygen is easy to overlook.
display.title: Is the plant's oxygen only for other organisms?
display.belief: The oxygen made by photosynthesis is for other organisms. The plant releases it into the air, not for itself.
display.evidence: Inside the same plant cell, oxygen made by chloroplasts diffuses to that cell's mitochondria and is used there in respiration. No delivery system sends oxygen only to other organisms; the gas is available to the cell that made it.
display.conclusion: The oxygen from photosynthesis is available to the plant's own respiration as well as to other organisms, and the plant also uses oxygen from the surrounding air.

accessibility.description: Misconception callout: the belief that photosynthesised oxygen is only for other organisms is tested by following oxygen from a cell's chloroplasts to its own mitochondria, and corrected by stating that the plant uses its own oxygen in respiration as well as releasing it to other organisms.

display.text:
**Photosynthesis in chloroplasts and respiration in mitochondria pass materials back and forth in a continuous cycle.**

Carbon dioxide and water enter the plant's chloroplasts, where light energy drives photosynthesis to produce glucose and oxygen. The glucose and oxygen travel to mitochondria in the plant's own cells and in the animal's cells, where respiration uses them and releases carbon dioxide and water.

Those products return to the chloroplasts as the inputs for photosynthesis. The oxygen made in photosynthesis is not only available to the animal; it is also available to the plant's own mitochondria for respiration. In the light, both processes run at the same time.

accessibility.description: Explains the cyclic exchange of materials between photosynthesis and respiration, including the plant's own use of its glucose and oxygen.

display.text: Respiration does not stop when light is available. Cells need a continuous supply of energy, so mitochondria keep using glucose and oxygen day and night. Photosynthesis, by contrast, can supply glucose and oxygen only when light is available. In bright light both processes run at the same time; in darkness only respiration runs. Inside the sealed tank, the plant and animal continue respiring during the dark phase, adding carbon dioxide and water that the plant will use when light returns.

items.body: **In a plant cell in light, photosynthesis and respiration run at the same time.** Chloroplasts trap light energy, build glucose and release oxygen. Mitochondria in the same cell use that glucose and oxygen, then release carbon dioxide and water. Those products are available to the chloroplasts, so each organelle supplies what the other needs.
items.title: Plant cell in light

items.body: Without light, chloroplasts cannot carry out photosynthesis, so no new glucose or oxygen is made. Mitochondria are not switched off: they keep using glucose and oxygen already present in the cell, and keep releasing carbon dioxide and water. Darkness removes the photosynthesis contribution only, so respiration carries on as before.
items.title: Plant cell in darkness

accessibility.description: A comparison of a plant cell in light with a plant cell in darkness. In light, chloroplasts and mitochondria are both active and exchange glucose, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water. In darkness, chloroplasts are inactive while mitochondria keep respiring.

display.caption: Plant cell in light with active chloroplasts and active mitochondria, showing glucose and oxygen from photosynthesis available to mitochondria and carbon dioxide and water from respiration available to chloroplasts. Plant cell in darkness with inactive chloroplasts and active mitochondria continuing to use glucose and oxygen and release carbon dioxide and water.

source_facts.text: Diagram of the sealed tank: carbon dioxide and water entering chloroplasts in the plant's cells; light energy driving photosynthesis in chloroplasts; glucose and oxygen produced by photosynthesis; glucose and oxygen used in mitochondria in the plant's cells and in the animal's cells; carbon dioxide and water produced by respiration; those products returning to the chloroplasts; and oxygen from photosynthesis available to the plant's own mitochondria as well as to the animal.

**Photosynthesis in chloroplasts and respiration in mitochondria pass materials back and forth in a continuous cycle.**

Carbon dioxide and water enter the plant's chloroplasts, where light energy drives photosynthesis to produce glucose and oxygen.
The glucose and oxygen travel to mitochondria in the plant's own cells and in the animal's cells, where respiration uses them and releases carbon dioxide and water.

display.aside: In a dark chamber the plant releases carbon dioxide and takes in oxygen, and in bright light those net changes reverse. That is why the take-turns idea feels convincing.
display.title: Do photosynthesis and respiration take turns?
display.belief: Photosynthesis happens in sunlight and respiration happens in darkness, so the plant switches from one to the other and only respires at night.
display.evidence: In a plant cell in bright light, the mitochondria are still taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide while the chloroplasts photosynthesise. Respiration has not switched off; light does not stop it.
display.conclusion: Respiration is continuous, day and night. Photosynthesis runs whenever light is available, so in the light both processes run at the same time in the same cell.

accessibility.description: Misconception callout: the belief that a plant respires only in darkness and photosynthesises only in light is tested against a plant cell in bright light, where mitochondria keep respiring, and corrected by stating that respiration is continuous while photosynthesis runs whenever light is available.

display.aside: Textbooks often describe plants releasing oxygen for animals, so the plant's own need for that oxygen is easy to overlook.
display.title: Is the plant's oxygen only for other organisms?
display.belief: The oxygen made by photosynthesis is for other organisms. The plant releases it into the air, not for itself.
display.evidence: Inside the same plant cell, oxygen made by chloroplasts diffuses to that cell's mitochondria and is used there in respiration. No delivery system sends oxygen only to other organisms; the gas is available to the cell that made it.
display.conclusion: The oxygen from photosynthesis is available to the plant's own respiration as well as to other organisms, and the plant also uses oxygen from the surrounding air.

accessibility.description: Misconception callout: the belief that photosynthesised oxygen is only for other organisms is tested by following oxygen from a cell's chloroplasts to its own mitochondria, and corrected by stating that the plant uses its own oxygen in respiration as well as releasing it to other organisms.

next_section.title: Why the 'take turns' and 'only for animals' ideas fail

items.body: **In a plant cell in light, photosynthesis and respiration run at the same time.** Chloroplasts trap light energy, build glucose and release oxygen. Mitochondria in the same cell use that glucose and oxygen, then release carbon dioxide and water. Those products are available to the chloroplasts, so each organelle supplies what the other needs.
items.title: Plant cell in light

items.body: Without light, chloroplasts cannot carry out photosynthesis, so no new glucose or oxygen is made. Mitochondria are not switched off: they keep using glucose and oxygen already present in the cell, and keep releasing carbon dioxide and water. Darkness removes the photosynthesis contribution only, so respiration carries on as before.
items.title: Plant cell in darkness

accessibility.description: A comparison of a plant cell in light with a plant cell in darkness. In light, chloroplasts and mitochondria are both active and exchange glucose, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water. In darkness, chloroplasts are inactive while mitochondria keep respiring.

display.caption: Plant cell in light with active chloroplasts and active mitochondria, showing glucose and oxygen from photosynthesis available to mitochondria and carbon dioxide and water from respiration available to chloroplasts. Plant cell in darkness with inactive chloroplasts and active mitochondria continuing to use glucose and oxygen and release carbon dioxide and water.

output_json.prompt: A student writes: "A plant's cells make glucose and oxygen during photosynthesis. The oxygen is released for animals, and the glucose is stored as starch. At night, the plant respires and uses the glucose and oxygen it stored during the day." Which correction should be made to this explanation?
output_json.purpose: check whether learners can correct an explanation that contains the alternating-process and oxygen-only-for-animals errors

feedback.correct: Respiration is continuous, and oxygen made by the plant's own photosynthesis is available to its own mitochondria as well as to other organisms.
feedback.incorrect: Recheck the two errors in the student's explanation: respiration does not happen only at night, and the plant's photosynthesised oxygen is also used by the plant itself.

options.text: Photosynthesis also supplies oxygen for the plant's own respiration, and respiration occurs continuously, not only at night.
The correction is that photosynthesis produces carbon dioxide and water, while respiration produces glucose and oxygen.
The correction is that the plant respires only during the day, because respiration requires the light energy captured by photosynthesis.
The correction is that oxygen made in photosynthesis is only for the plant itself, and no oxygen is available to other organisms.

option_notes.a: Corrects both target errors: respiration is continuous and the plant uses its own photosynthesised oxygen.
option_notes.b: Reverses the inputs and outputs of photosynthesis and respiration.
option_notes.c: Claims respiration occurs only in the day, which retains the alternating-process error.
option_notes.d: States oxygen is only for the plant, the opposite imbalance to the student's oxygen-only-for-animals error.

output_json.expected_evidence: the learner selects the correction that states respiration uses glucose and oxygen continuously, including oxygen made by the plant's own photosynthesis, rather than only at night or only for animals
